headline.main: Executive-Ordered Out of Existence: How Trump's Transphobia Is Affecting My Family from Afar
headline.social: Executive-Ordered Out of Existence: How Trump's Transphobia Is Affecting My Family from Afar

intro: My transgender daughter is getting the care she needs here in Berlin. But she is no longer able to travel to her second home in the U.S. to visit family and friends. In Donald Trump's America, the transgender community is under attack. And the consequences could be devastating.
text:
The woman at the registry office in the Schöneberg district of Berlin couldn’t have been more supportive and understanding. She even tried – despite the emphatically bureaucratic backdrop of shelves packed with three-ring binders, file cabinets stacked with documents and numerous stamps dangling expectantly from a well-used stamp carousel to the right of her keyboard – to inject a bit of ceremony into the moment.
"Many people,” she said with a smile on her face, "treat it as their second birthday. Congratulations.”
She then handed us a sheaf of papers with which the German state officially recognized my 15-year-old transgender daughter’s identity and paved the way for her sex and name to be changed on her German passport and ID. She even got a brand-new birth certificate.
To celebrate the moment, we walked outside to the portico of the Schöneberg City Hall and took a selfie with the plastic, tuxedo-clad Berlin bear standing on the top step, smiles on our faces and hopeful that this day might alleviate at least some of the wrenching angst that gender dysphoria has wrought on our daughter.
The happiness of that moment in late February, however, was not unclouded. My daughter, as it happens, is also a citizen of the United States. And the U.S., under the leadership of Donald Trump and backed by an obsequious Republican Party, no longer officially recognizes the existence of transgender people like my daughter and demands that their "identity” papers reflect their sex assigned at birth.
That hostility, combined with the uncertainty of what might happen were my daughter to turn up at the U.S. border with two different passports using two different names and two different genders – not to mention the shock to her already fragile psyche that would likely ensue when confronted by unsympathetic officials using her deadname – means that for the foreseeable future, we cannot travel as a family to the United States to visit grandma, uncles, aunts, cousins and friends.
A Rejection of Her Very Existence
My daughter, in other words, has been declared persona non grata.
The direct and immediate implications for my family are painful. I have always sought to give my two children – my daughter is joined by an 11-year-old son – the opportunity to develop a close relationship with the country where I grew up and the people I grew up with. Our mostly annual trips to the West Coast have long been a highlight of our year – hiking the mountains of the Cascades near grandma’s home in Bend, Oregon, visiting friends in Seattle, whale watching on the beautiful islands dotting Puget Sound, rock climbing at Smith Rock and marveling at the beauty of the Columbia River Gorge. Those are all things that we can no longer experience as a family.
For the family, it is a bitter pill to swallow. For my daughter, it feels like a rejection of her very existence.
Still, our family’s plight is a far cry from the situation now being faced by tens of thousands of transgender people and families of transgender children in other countries. In Britain, the Supreme Court has just ruled that a woman is only a woman if that was her biologically assigned sex at birth. In the United States, they have been told in no uncertain terms that they are unwanted. And for many of them, the effects of the Republican Party’s onslaught on transgender people are far more immediate.
That onslaught, it should be noted, was launched well before Trump was sworn in on January 20, 2025. Since 2021, the number of anti-trans bills under consideration in state legislatures around the country have skyrocketed. Whereas 143 bills were considered that year, according to the Trans Legislation Tracker , fully 830 of them are under consideration this year, an increase of 480 percent – the vast majority of them in states where Republicans are in charge.
They include bans on gender-affirming care for youths (such care is now illegal in more than half of the 50 states), bans on LGBTQ+ flags being displayed at schools, laws making it illegal for teachers to discuss sexual orientation and gender identity, mandates that restrooms only be labeled as "men” or "women,” bans on transgender women and girls from participating on sports teams consistent with their gender, directives that transgender women convicts be held in male-only prisons… The list goes on.
Trump, though, decided that wasn’t enough. Despite their making up just 0.6 percent of the population, Trump decided to ramp up the assault on America’s transgender community on the very first day of his second term in the White House. The executive order he signed – carrying the disingenuous name "Defending Women From Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government” – mandates that only two sexes exist and they are biologically determined at birth. The "X” designation is no longer allowed.
More executive orders attacking transgender people have followed, and the federal government has moved to deny the issuing of new passports to trans and nonbinary Americans. It has moved to strongarm hospitals into ceasing gender-affirming care for minors even in states where it remains legal. It has banned transgender men and women from serving in the military. And it has slashed funding for LGBTQ+ programs.
The White House has even sought to erase transgender people entirely, purging federal websites of all mention of transgender and deleting valuable research into LGBTQ+ health and social issues from federal websites. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the State Department have removed the term transgender from their homepages.
The situation is so aggressively deleterious for transgender people that several European countries, including Germany, have issued travel advisories warning transgender people against visiting the United States.
Again, our family has thankfully been spared from the most onerous effects of this blitz. Germany is one of the best countries in the world for transgender people to live in, with the Self-Determination Act – the one that allowed my daughter to align her gender with her identity and to change her name – going into effect on November 1, 2024, and gender-affirming care is available and covered by health insurance.
But even here – living in a country that understands that gender dysphoria is a real condition requiring real care, living in a city that is extremely tolerant of transgender youth and being part of a generation that is phenomenally accepting of all LGBTQ+ identities – our daughter’s path has been far from smooth.
We have witnessed up close just how agonizing it can be for those experiencing gender dysphoria, even absent political obstacles and federally mandated malevolence. Depression, suicidal thoughts, self-harm: All of those things are present at a far higher rate among transgender youth than they are among their cisgender peers. They are – in Germany as elsewhere – the constant companions of many families with transgender children.
Skyrocketing Suicide Rates
Which is why, not long after taking that family selfie on the front steps of the Schöneberg City Hall, I found myself thinking less about the fact that our family trips to the United States were coming to an end and more about the research showing that suicide attempts among transgender and nonbinary youth in the U.S. have rocketed upwards in recent years, in lockstep with the number of laws being passed against them. I found myself worrying about all those kids who are now being denied the gender-affirming care they so badly need. I found myself wondering about the reports of transgender families seeking asylum in Canada.
And I also found myself thinking of a different U.S. president. It was right there, on the very steps of the building where we stood with the Berlin bear, that John F. Kennedy gave his famous "Ich bin ein Berliner” speech.
It was just one of his many influential speeches. In another, delivered on a different occasion, he said: "Every American ought to have the right to be treated as he would wish to be treated, as one would wish his children to be treated.”
The gendering might be outdated. But the message, in Donald Trump's America, is needed more than ever.
